newsitem.title: USA: U.S. securities execs meet, celebrate record year.
newsitem.headline: U.S. securities execs meet, celebrate record year.

text.p: With the Securities Industry Association's annual meeting about to convene, hundreds of executives are headed to balmy Boca Raton, Florida to congratulate themselves on another record year.
However, with a bevy of regulatory issues on the horizon and the outcome of the national elections to digest, attendees are unlikely to focus too long on the rear-view mirror.
Participants like New York Stock Exchange chairman and chief executive Richard Grasso and and Securities and Exchange Commission chairman Arthur Levitt will draw close attention.

"It's important to listen to what non-industry members like Grasso and anybody from the SEC have to say," said Perrin Long, an independent analyst covering securities firms. "What they say can have long-term implications for the industry."

The meeting which convenes Wednesday and ends Saturday, will no doubt devote some attention to the undeniable industry successes of 1996, such as the record pace of mergers and initial public offerings. Of course, many will question whether the industry can duplicate its results next year; at least one panel will discuss the outlook for the economy and markets.

Panelists will include Abby Joseph Cohen, co-chair of Goldman Sachs & Co's investment policy committee, Gail Dudack, chief investment strategist at UBS Securities, and Byron Wein, Morgan Stanley's top U.S. investment strategist.
"Mini-conferences" during the meeting will address securities legislation and regulation, as well as federal fiscal and tax policy. A panel discussion of the 1996 election results is also scheduled.
Technology will also occupy center stage, as securities and technology executives explore topics like the increasing use of the Internet for brokerage and research distribution.
Featured technology executives will include Henry Schacht, chairman of Lucent Technologies Inc and Scott Cook, chairman of Intuit Inc.

Among this year's highlights, according to the SIA's figures, the 603 initial public offerings through September alone exceeded 1995's figure by five percent and the annualized rate of initial offerings of $46.9 billion is 56 percent higher than 1995's total and 13 percent higher than 1993's record amount.
Merger and acquisition activity is also booming, with the SIA estimating total deal volume for 1996 at about $496 billion, nearly triple 1993 levels.
